name: Abi Aryan
title: Reliability Engineering for Inference Serving
abstract: Training gave us powerful models, but inference is where the real production battle begins. Agentic workflows are burning money by the second, GPU economics are tightening each quarter, and a single unpredictable latency tail or silent kernel failure can turn a working system into an outage. Reliability thus is no longer just about uptime.This keynote is a call to SREs, GPU engineers, and LLMOps practitioners. I’ll share some of the hard lessons, emerging patterns, and new rules shaping the next decade of reliable AI systems
bio: Abi Aryan is the founder of Abide AI, educator and author of the O'Reilly book LLMOps and an upcoming book in GPU Engineering. With over 10 years of experience productionizing AI/ML systems and prior research experience at UCLA under Dr. Judea Pearl, she has been focusing on making AI systems reliable, observable, and sustainable at scale.

name: Viktor Vasylkovskyi
title: Multi-Agent Architectures - What we shipped, what broke, and what we'd do differently
abstract: I've been building production AI agents with LangGraph - sometimes getting it right, often learning the hard way. This talk is about what I actually shipped, including a distributed multi-agent setup at PagerDuty. I'll break down the real tradeoffs between LLM-driven and deterministic orchestration, what broke, and how I'd approach it differently now.

name: Fabricio De los Santos
title: The Next Step
abstract:
In AI and LLM projects, we often talk about big ideas. But in my experience, the real difficulty is not always having the idea. It is knowing what to do next.
When an idea feels too big, too abstract, or too ambitious, it is easy to postpone it, overbuild it, or create a demo that looks interesting but does not solve a real problem. In this talk, I would like to share a simple way of thinking that has helped me in real automation, integration, and LLM projects: instead of asking only “Will this idea work?”, I try to ask “What is the next step I can take to validate it?”
That next step can be a small prototype, a manual test, a workflow with an LLM, a conversation with users, or even the conclusion that AI is not necessary yet. I will share practical lessons from building AI workflows, assistants, and enterprise automations, including some doubts, mistakes, and decisions that usually happen before an idea becomes a real product.
The goal is not to present a perfect formula, but to open a conversation with the community about how we can move from AI enthusiasm to useful experiments, without losing focus or control.
bio: Fabricio De los Santos is an AI Solutions & Integration Architect with more than 25 years of experience in enterprise software, system integrations, automation, and applied AI across LATAM and Europe. His work combines practical LLM integrations, RAG, APIs, FastAPI, n8n, low-code experience, and real production projects. He is also an author and writes about AI, technology, and human decision-making.

name: Afonso Oliveira
title: How Far Can You Go With AI Without Sharing Your Data?
abstract:
We've learned to expect privacy from the tools we use. Signal, Proton, and others have shown that companies can build real products while proving they never see your data. But what about AI?
For users handing over their most personal questions, and for companies sitting on sensitive data, third-party APIs are something to avoid. The most useful AI is often the AI they can't safely use. Is running everything locally the only answer?
We'll start there, looking at how far local and edge AI have come and where it breaks down. But even with cost and scale out of the way, imagine a company that has a good value-add and wants to ship AI features while preserving privacy. Following in Signal and Proton's steps, they'd have to expose all their hard work: fine-tuned model weights, agentic systems, and more.
Current solutions for processing private data remotely exist, but they're not part of your everyday dev feed. We'll work through the techniques that close the gap: from computing on encrypted data to hardware-isolated enclaves, weighing how deep your trust needs to go, the tools you can reach for today, and what's coming next.
bio: Afonso Oliveira has spent 14 years figuring out how to make AI useful. He first applied this in research, earning a PhD with honors from Instituto Superior Técnico on neural networks for 5G resource allocation, then brought that rigor into product development. Somewhere along the way he also co-founded a startup, won a few international hackathons, and wrote a chapter in a book on AI published by ISCTE.

name: Tetiana Torovets
title: The Platform Moment for Agents: Standardizing AI Development at Scale
abstract:
Building the first AI agent is easy. The real challenge begins when dozens of teams start building dozens of agents.
As organizations scale their AI investments, teams naturally optimize for speed and autonomy. They choose different frameworks, define their own tool interfaces, implement memory differently, create custom evaluation approaches, and establish their own operational practices. Each decision makes sense locally.
The problems emerge when the organization wants these agents to collaborate.
Capabilities developed by multiple teams become difficult to combine. Integrations become expensive. Evaluations become incomparable. Observability becomes fragmented. Innovation slows as every new initiative requires custom glue between incompatible systems.
In this talk, I will discuss why agentic development is reaching its platform moment. Drawing on lessons from scaling AI products and platforms in large organizations, I will explore the standards, interfaces, and architectural principles that enable teams to innovate independently while remaining interoperable. We will cover common patterns for tool integration, memory, evaluation, observability, and governance, as well as the organizational challenges that emerge as AI adoption grows.
The future challenge is not building more agents. It is enabling agents built by different teams to work together.
bio: Tetiana Torovets is a data science and AI leader with more than 10 years of experience building and scaling machine learning products. name: Xavier Anguera
title: Your DIY AI companion
abstract:
Conversational AI has quietly become the most intimate form of human–computer interaction we have ever built. From character.ai companions racking up billions of messages, to AI tutors that hold a child's attention longer than any app before them, talking to a machine no longer feels like science fiction - it feels routine. But behind every smooth conversation lies a stack of design decisions: how do you keep latency under the threshold where it stops feeling human? How do you let users interrupt mid-sentence? Do you bet on a single end-to-end speech model, or stitch together ASR, an LLM, and TTS like classic plumbing?
In this talk we'll tour the landscape of conversational AI — its breakout applications, its risks (especially in companion and edtech use cases), and the two architectural schools fighting for the future. Then we'll roll up our sleeves and build one. Live, on a laptop, for free, walking through every block of a modern voice agent. You'll leave with a block diagram in your head, a list of swappable components, and a ready-to-code spec you can hand to Claude Code tonight to ship your own AI companion before bedtime.
bio: Xavier Anguera is SVP of AI for Language Learning at Babbel and a recognised expert in Speech AI, Deep Learning, and Large Language Models. name: Scott Bastek
title: Teaching AI Systems to Fix Their Own Failures
abstract: Prompt engineering has traditionally been manual trial-and-error. When AI agents degrade in production, teams make gut-feel changes and hope for the best. How do you know if a prompt change actually improves things, or just shifts failures elsewhere? We built an automated system that transforms production failures into quantifiable fixes. It starts by fetching examples of suboptimal sessions from our observability platform. The system analyzes these failures and clusters them into actionable patterns. For each pattern, it proposes specific prompt changes with before-and-after text. Then comes the critical step: validation. Only improvements that maintain or boost performance against our golden dataset make it into an automated pull request. Finally, the golden dataset itself is updated with representative samples of assessed failure. The result? We analyze all failures weekly and ship validated fixes—all without manual debugging. This approach transforms vague ""my AI isn't working"" complaints into concrete, measurable improvements backed by production data.
bio: Scott Bastek is a Data Science professional at PagerDuty with a background from MIT. Based in Lisbon, he focuses on applying data science and modern AI techniques to solve practical engineering and operational challenges.

name: Marcelo Ventura
title: My Life Before and After LLMs
abstract:
Almost ten years ago I was a data scientist who memorized APIs, read papers to find a gap, and scoped every project to what I could personally code. Today I write less code than ever and ship more software than ever — across research, data work, building a company, navigating immigration, and helping my family.
This is five short before/after stories with one shared shape: where my thinking used to start, where it starts now, and the skill I quietly stopped exercising in exchange. No architecture diagrams — instead, the human version of a problem many of us are solving in our systems: when producing work gets cheap and verifying it gets expensive, do we upgrade our judgment as fast as our tools?
I'll use real examples — from RAG-based legal assistants to building imigrei.pt and Prep Docs to help immigrants face Portuguese bureaucracy—and close with an uncomfortable question. You'll leave having relocated at least one bottleneck in your own workflow, and a little unsure whether you're still good at the part that now matters most.
bio: Marcelo Ventura is a data scientist and AI engineer based in Lisbon. Over nearly a decade he has built ML and data systems across Brazil, Singapore, New York, California, and Central Europe — from loan-forecasting neural nets and cashflow automation to RAG-based GenAI assistants and legal copilots at fintechs and startups. He holds an MSc in Applied Economics and has published research in statistical modeling and econometrics. A Brazilian immigrant himself, he is now Data & AI Engineer at imigrei.pt, where he builds tools — including Prep Docs — that help immigrants navigate Portuguese bureaucracy, and hosts the Imigrantes de Sucesso podcast.

name: Aleksandr Kamenev
title: Shipping Production Software Solo with Claude Code
abstract:
Most "I built an app with AI" stories stop at the prototype. This talk is about the harder part: taking an agentic coding tool from a working demo to software you can put real users on and maintain by yourself. I'll use app.smarthostinghub.com — a production app I designed, built, and run single-handedly — as the running case study, with a quick live look at how it's structured.
The core idea: once the model can write the code, the bottleneck moves to context and verification. So I'll focus on just three things that make solo agentic development hold up in production:
- Set the context first: a written spec, data model, and a CLAUDE.md / docs layer that act as the agent's memory — because any rule you don't write down, it will silently break.
- Ship in small, reviewable slices: every feature end-to-end (data → API → UI → test) in chunks small enough to actually review, with types and tests as the gate that stops bad code from merging.
- Keep humans on the risky seams: auth, billing, and database migrations stay under explicit review, never on autopilot.
Then the honest part: what broke, and what I'd do differently now. Attendees leave with a short checklist they can apply to their own projects the next day.
bio: Aleksandr Kamenev is the founder and CEO of NerdHeadz (nerdheadz.com), a Wyoming-registered AI and custom software development agency; he's based in Lisbon. Over ~12 years in software he's moved from enterprise development to leading a distributed team that has shipped 60+ projects, and today he spends much of his time building and running production applications single-handedly with agentic coding tools. Trained as a radio engineer, he bootstrapped NerdHeadz past seven figures in revenue without outside funding.

name: Rahul Kumar
title: How to build and use Second Brain.
abstract: Most people talk about AI tools. I want to talk about the thing that makes them actually work i.e. Memory. Not the model, not the prompt, the persistent knowledge layer underneath it all. I'll walk through how high-performers are building their second brain: a structured, queryable layer of their own thinking that compounds over time. I'll cover what actually needs to go in (and what doesn't), how to design it so an LLM can reason over it, and what this looks like in practice for founders, consultants, and operators running on context-switching overload.
bio: AI practitioner with 14+ years in the field, 2x published author (Packt), Techstars alumni, and founder of Timeln. I've delivered production ready AI systems across BFSI, Telecom, O&G, Healthcare, and ad tech.

name: Philipp Pahl
title: Teaching Your Agent's Search Engine to Listen: Fine Tuning Retrieval on Proprietary Data
abstract:
AI agents don't search like humans. They reason between every search call, and unlike humans, they're not lazy about spelling it out: what worked, what didn't, what to look for next. That chain of thought is rich retrieval signal that today's search engines throw away.
Late interaction retrieval models can exploit that signal. Unlike single vector embeddings, which compress an entire document into one point in space, late interaction keeps a vector per token, capturing far more nuance with far smaller models. The tradeoff is more compute at search time, but efficient indexing techniques have largely solved that. And because these models are comparably small, they're fast and cheap to fine tune for your domain. That matters especially when you work with proprietary or specialized data where off the shelf models fall short: a generic retriever has never seen your internal documents, your terminology, your relevance criteria. Fine tuning bridges that gap.
That's where frontier LLMs change the game. Training a retriever for your domain used to mean hiring annotators. Today, frontier models judge relevance at human evaluator quality and smaller, more affordable models can handle many of the same tasks at a fraction of the cost. I'll walk through a reproducible recipe: pool candidates with cheap retrievers, rerank them with LLM judges, extract training pairs. Then fine tune a late interaction model in minutes on a single rented GPU.
